Self-Attention and the Transformer

The transformer, introduced in 2017, replaced recurrence with self-attention: every token can look directly at every other token in one step. This parallelism is why modern LLMs scale.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Imagine each word in a sentence shouting a question and listening for the most relevant answers from all the other words. Attention decides who to listen to and how loudly.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Each token is projected into three vectors: a Query (Q), a Key (K), and a Value (V). Attention scores come from the dot product Q·K, scaled by the square root of the key dimension, then passed through softmax to get weights that sum to 1. Those weights blend the Values.

scores = (Q @ K.T) / sqrt(d_k)\nweights = softmax(scores)\noutput  = weights @ V

Multi-head attention runs several Q/K/V projections in parallel so different heads capture different relationships (syntax, coreference, position). Outputs are concatenated and projected. Each block also adds a position-wise feed-forward network, residual connections, and layer normalization.

📝 KEY IDEA

The scaling factor 1/√d_k keeps dot products from growing large, which would push softmax into saturated regions with vanishing gradients.

Because attention is permutation-invariant, transformers add positional information (sinusoidal or rotary/RoPE embeddings) so order matters. Decoder-only LLMs use a causal mask so a token cannot attend to future positions during next-token prediction.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Vanilla self-attention costs O(n²) in sequence length. Long contexts are expensive, which is why FlashAttention and sparse/linear variants exist — attention is not free just because it is parallel.

📊 FIGURE — the shapes inside one head
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Why the mask must come before the softmax

Shape first. Q is n × d_k and Kᵀ is d_k × n, so QKᵀ is n × n — for 10 tokens, a 10 × 10 matrix holding one score for every ordered pair of positions. Doubling the sequence quadruples this matrix, which is the whole reason long context is expensive.

Now the masking. Setting a masked score to −∞ makes its exponential zero, and the softmax then renormalises what remains so the surviving weights still sum to 1.

Masking after the softmax would zero some weights that had already been counted in the denominator, leaving the rest summing to less than 1 — the output would be a shrunken, arbitrarily scaled mix rather than a proper weighted average. So the mask goes in before, while the normalisation can still account for it.

🎯 EXAM TIP
QKᵀ is n × n — 10 tokens give a 10 × 10 score matrix. And the causal mask is added before the softmax, because −∞ scores exponentiate to zero and let the softmax renormalise; zeroing weights afterwards would leave them summing to less than 1.

Turning Text into Numbers

Models never see letters; they see integer token IDs. Tokenization splits text into subword units, and an embedding table maps each ID to a learned vector.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Tokenization is like chopping a sentence into LEGO bricks of common word-pieces. Rare words get built from small bricks; common words are single bricks.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) starts from bytes/characters and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token, building a vocabulary of a fixed size (often 30k–200k). This keeps the vocabulary bounded while handling any string, including emoji and code.

For example, tokenization might split into token + ization, while a rare name splits into many pieces. This is why token counts differ from word counts, and why non-English or code text can cost more tokens.

📝 KEY IDEA

Each token ID indexes a row in the embedding matrix. Those vectors are learned, so semantically similar tokens drift toward similar directions in the vector space.

  • Vocabulary size: bigger vocab = fewer tokens per sentence but a larger embedding table.
  • Special tokens: markers like end-of-sequence or role delimiters are added to the vocabulary.
  • Embeddings: dimension d (e.g., 4096) is the model's working width.
⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Do not equate one token with one word. On average English is roughly 0.75 words per token, but numbers, whitespace, and code fragment heavily — always measure with the model's actual tokenizer before estimating cost or context limits.

Adapting Models Efficiently

Full fine-tuning updates every weight of a model — powerful but memory-hungry. Parameter-efficient methods change only a tiny slice while freezing the rest.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Instead of repainting an entire house, LoRA adds a thin, cheap overlay on a few walls. The original structure stays frozen; you only tune the overlay.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) freezes the pretrained weight matrix W and learns two small matrices A and B such that the update is ΔW = B·A, where A and B have a low rank r (e.g., 8 or 16). Only A and B are trained, cutting trainable parameters by orders of magnitude. At inference you can merge B·A back into W for zero added latency.

h = W0 @ x + (B @ A) @ x   # W0 frozen; A, B trainable, rank r
📝 KEY IDEA

QLoRA goes further: it loads the frozen base model in 4-bit (NF4) quantization and trains LoRA adapters in higher precision on top. This lets you fine-tune very large models on a single GPU.

Key LoRA hyperparameters: rank r (capacity), alpha (scaling of the update), target modules (often the attention Q/V projections), and dropout. QLoRA adds double quantization and paged optimizers to save more memory.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

LoRA does not add new knowledge for free — it adapts style, format, and task behavior. If the base model truly lacks a capability, a low rank cannot conjure it, and setting rank far too small underfits the task.

Making Inference Cheap and Fast

Quantization stores model weights (and sometimes activations) in fewer bits — 8-bit, 4-bit, even lower — instead of 16- or 32-bit floats. Smaller weights mean less memory and faster memory-bound inference.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

It is like saving a photo as a smaller JPEG: you lose a little detail to make the file much smaller and quicker to load. Done well, you barely notice.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Weights are mapped from a floating-point range to a small set of integers using a scale (and optional zero-point). Post-training quantization (PTQ) methods like GPTQ and AWQ calibrate on sample data to minimize error; quantization-aware training simulates rounding during training for higher fidelity.

📝 KEY IDEA

LLM inference is often memory-bandwidth bound, not compute bound. Shrinking weights lets more of the model fit in fast memory and reduces bytes moved per token, which is why 4-bit models can serve faster.

Beyond quantization, throughput techniques include the KV cache (store past keys/values so each new token is cheap), continuous batching (pack many requests together), speculative decoding, and FlashAttention.

  • INT8: near-lossless for most models.
  • 4-bit (NF4/GPTQ/AWQ): large memory savings, small quality drop.
  • Below 4-bit: savings shrink while quality loss grows.
⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Quantization is a tradeoff, not free. Aggressive low-bit quantization can degrade reasoning and rare-token accuracy, and outlier activations may need special handling — always evaluate the quantized model on your task.

Semantic Search with Vectors

An embedding model turns text into a fixed-length vector so that meaning becomes geometry: similar texts land close together. A vector database stores millions of these vectors and finds the nearest ones fast.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Think of every document as a pin on a giant map of meaning. Ask a question, drop a pin for it, and the nearest pins are the most relevant documents.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Relevance is measured by cosine similarity — the angle between vectors — or dot product / Euclidean distance. Because comparing against every vector is slow, vector DBs use Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) indexes like HNSW or IVF that trade a little recall for large speedups.

query_vec = embed(\"how do I reset my password?\")\nresults   = index.search(query_vec, top_k=5, metric=\"cosine\")
📝 KEY IDEA

Cosine similarity ignores vector magnitude and compares direction, so it is robust to length. Many pipelines normalize vectors, making cosine and dot product equivalent.

Vector DBs (e.g., pgvector, Pinecone, Weaviate, Qdrant, FAISS) also support metadata filtering so you can combine semantic search with structured constraints like date or author.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

You must query with the same embedding model used to index. Mixing models, or comparing across incompatible vector spaces, yields meaningless similarities and silently bad retrieval.

Chunking Documents for Retrieval

Before you can retrieve, you must split documents into chunks that are small enough to embed precisely but large enough to stay meaningful. Chunking quality often matters more than the choice of vector DB.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Cutting a book into index cards: too-big cards blur many topics together; too-small cards lose context. You want each card to hold one coherent idea.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Common strategies: fixed-size chunks (e.g., 500 tokens) with an overlap of 10–20% so ideas that straddle a boundary aren't lost; recursive splitting on structure (headings, paragraphs, sentences); and semantic chunking that breaks where embedding similarity drops.

📝 KEY IDEA

Overlap trades storage for safety: repeating a little text between adjacent chunks prevents a query from falling into a gap where the answer was split across a boundary.

To improve search, teams combine dense (embedding) retrieval with sparse keyword search (BM25) in a hybrid pipeline, then apply a reranker (a cross-encoder) to reorder the top candidates by true relevance.

  • Too large: dilutes the embedding, drags in irrelevant text.
  • Too small: loses context, fragments answers.
  • Metadata: attach source, section, and titles to each chunk.
⚠️ COMMON TRAP

One giant chunk per document seems simple but wrecks precision: the query matches a broad average vector, and the model then wades through mostly irrelevant text, raising cost and hallucination risk.

Retrieval-Augmented Generation End to End

RAG grounds an LLM in your data: retrieve relevant chunks, insert them into the prompt as context, and ask the model to answer using only that context. It reduces hallucination and keeps answers current without retraining.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

It's an open-book exam. The model still writes the answer, but you hand it the right pages first so it doesn't guess from memory.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Pipeline: (1) embed and index your corpus; (2) at query time, embed the question and retrieve top-k chunks; (3) build a prompt with the chunks; (4) the LLM generates a grounded, ideally cited answer.

Context:\n{retrieved_chunks}\n\nQuestion: {user_question}\nAnswer using ONLY the context above; cite sources.
📝 KEY IDEA

Evaluate the two halves separately. Retrieval quality: metrics like recall@k, precision@k, and MRR. Generation quality: faithfulness (is the answer supported by the context?) and answer relevance (does it address the question?).

Tools like RAGAS use an LLM-as-judge to score faithfulness and context relevance. A frequent fix for wrong answers is better retrieval or chunking, not a bigger model.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Garbage retrieval in, garbage answer out. If the right chunk is never retrieved, no prompt engineering saves the answer — always diagnose retrieval before blaming the generator.

📊 FIGURE — citations in a RAG system
🎯 EXAM TIP
Requiring the model to cite the retrieved chunk supporting each claim primarily makes unsupported claims auditable, so hallucinations can be detected. Be precise about the mechanism: citations do not stop the model inventing things — they convert a silent invention into a visible mismatch between claim and source.

From Chatbots to Agents

An agent is an LLM placed in a loop where it can take actions, observe results, and decide what to do next — rather than answering in a single shot. The classic pattern is ReAct: interleave Reasoning and Acting.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A plain chatbot answers from memory. An agent is more like a detective: think, gather a clue (act), look at it (observe), think again — repeat until the case is solved.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

The ReAct loop cycles through Thought → Action → Observation. The model writes a thought, chooses a tool and inputs (Action), the system runs it and returns the result (Observation), and the loop continues until the model emits a final answer.

Thought: I need today's weather in Paris.\nAction: get_weather(city=\"Paris\")\nObservation: 18C, cloudy\nThought: I can now answer.\nFinal Answer: It's 18C and cloudy in Paris.
📝 KEY IDEA

Reasoning traces let the model plan and self-correct, while actions let it access fresh, external, or precise information the weights don't contain. The combination beats either alone.

Agents need a stopping condition and a step budget; otherwise they loop. Frameworks add orchestration, tool schemas, and error handling around this core loop.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Without a max-step limit or clear termination, an agent can loop forever, repeat the same failing action, or burn tokens. Always cap steps and handle tool errors explicitly.

Function Calling and Tool Use

Function calling lets an LLM request an external operation by emitting structured arguments that match a declared schema. The model doesn't run code — it decides which function to call and with what arguments.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

The model fills out an order form: it names the tool and the fields, hands the form to your app, and your app does the actual work, then reports back.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

You provide tool definitions — name, description, and a JSON Schema of parameters. The model returns a tool call with JSON arguments; your code executes it and returns the result, which the model uses to continue.

{\n  \"name\": \"get_weather\",\n  \"description\": \"Current weather for a city\",\n  \"parameters\": {\n    \"type\": \"object\",\n    \"properties\": { \"city\": {\"type\": \"string\"} },\n    \"required\": [\"city\"]\n  }\n}
📝 KEY IDEA

Clear tool descriptions and well-typed schemas are the interface: the model chooses tools based on them, so good naming and constraints dramatically improve reliability.

Modern APIs support parallel tool calls and enforce structured JSON output. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes how agents connect to external tools and data sources.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

The model can hallucinate arguments or call the wrong tool. Never blindly execute — validate arguments against the schema, sandbox side effects, and require confirmation for irreversible actions.

Planning and Memory

Complex tasks need more than a reactive loop. Agents plan — decomposing a goal into steps — and use memory to carry information beyond the current context window.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Planning is writing a to-do list before starting; memory is the notebook you keep so you don't forget what you learned three tasks ago.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Planning strategies include decomposition (break a goal into subtasks), plan-and-execute (draft a full plan, then run it), and reflection (critique and revise after acting). Memory splits into short-term (the current context window / scratchpad) and long-term (an external store, often a vector DB, retrieved when relevant).

📝 KEY IDEA

Long-term memory is usually implemented as retrieval: write summaries or facts to a store, then pull the most relevant ones back into context — the same machinery as RAG, applied to the agent's own history.

Because context is finite and costly, agents summarize or compress old turns and keep only salient facts. Episodic memory records past interactions; semantic memory holds distilled knowledge.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Dumping the entire history into the prompt doesn't scale: it inflates cost, hits context limits, and buries key facts. Selective retrieval and summarization beat brute-force stuffing.

Coordinating Multiple Agents

Some problems are easier with several specialized agents than one generalist. Multi-agent systems divide work across roles that communicate to reach a goal.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Like a project team: a manager assigns tasks, specialists do the work, and a reviewer checks quality — each person focused on what they do best.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Common topologies: an orchestrator (supervisor) that routes subtasks to worker agents and merges results; a pipeline where each agent's output feeds the next; and debate/critic setups where agents review one another. Each agent has its own role, tools, and prompt.

📝 KEY IDEA

Specialization plus clear interfaces reduces each agent's cognitive load and context size, often improving reliability over a single monolithic prompt trying to do everything.

Coordination needs a shared protocol: message passing, a common scratchpad or blackboard, and a way to decide who acts next. A supervisor pattern centralizes control; a decentralized pattern lets agents hand off directly.

  • Supervisor: central routing and aggregation.
  • Pipeline: sequential specialization.
  • Critic: review and refine outputs.
⚠️ COMMON TRAP

More agents is not always better: extra communication multiplies token cost and latency, and errors can cascade between agents. Add agents only when the task genuinely decomposes into distinct roles.

Attention, Scaling, and Memory

\n

Scaled dot-product attention computes Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k)V. Q,K,V are n×d_k. The QKᵀ product is n×n and dominates cost.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
\n
⚙️ FORMULAS\n
    \n
  • Attention time: O(n²·d) (QKᵀ and scores·V each n²d). Memory for scores: O(n²) per head.
    • \n
  • KV-cache bytes = 2 · n_layers · n_ctx · d_model · bytes (2 = K and V).
    • \n
  • Transformer block params ≈ 12·d² (4d² attention QKVO + 8d² MLP with d_ff=4d).
    • \n
  • LoRA trainable params for one w∈ℝ^(d×k) at rank r: r·(d+k); square d×d ⇒ 2dr.
    • \n
  • FLOPs/token ≈ 2N (forward), 6N (training) where N = param count.
    • \n
\n
💡 KEY RESULTS\n
    \n
  • √d_k scaling keeps the dot-product variance ≈1 so softmax does not saturate into near-one-hot gradient-killing regions.
    • \n
  • KV-cache and score memory grow linearly and quadratically in context length respectively — context is the memory bottleneck at inference.
    • \n
  • 4-bit weights ≈ 0.5 byte/param; fp16 = 2; fp32 = 4; int8 = 1.
    • \n
\n
⚠️ SUBTLETY\n

FlashAttention keeps compute at O(n²·d) but reduces memory to O(n) by never materializing the full n×n score matrix — it does not change the asymptotic FLOP count.

\n
📝 TECHNIQUE\n

QLoRA loads the frozen base in NF4 4-bit (memory = params×0.5B) and trains only small LoRA adapters in bf16, cutting fine-tune memory by roughly 4× vs fp16 full weights.

Vector Retrieval, Ranking, and Cost

\n

Dense retrieval embeds queries and chunks into ℝ^d and ranks by cosine similarity cos(a,b)=a·b/(‖a‖‖b‖). Normalized embeddings make cosine equal to dot product, so inner-product ANN indexes suffice.

\n
⚙️ FORMULAS\n
    \n
  • Recall@k = (relevant items in top-k) / (total relevant).
    • \n
  • Reciprocal Rank = 1/(rank of first relevant); MRR = mean over queries.
    • \n
  • DCG@k = Σ relᵢ / log₂(i+1); nDCG@k = DCG/IDCG (IDCG = DCG of ideal ordering).
    • \n
  • Fixed-stride chunking: stride = chunk − overlap; #chunks = ⌈(L−chunk)/stride⌉ + 1.
    • \n
\n
💡 KEY RESULTS\n
    \n
  • HNSW trades recall for latency via M (graph degree) and efSearch (candidate list): higher values raise recall and cost.
    • \n
  • Retrieving more chunks eventually hurts: irrelevant context dilutes attention (\"lost in the middle\") and raises token cost.
    • \n
  • Cross-encoder reranking is accurate but O(k) forward passes — retrieve wide with cheap ANN, rerank narrow.
    • \n
\n
⚠️ SUBTLETY\n

Recall@k measures whether relevant docs are retrieved at all; nDCG rewards ranking them high. A retriever can have high recall@20 yet poor nDCG@5 if relevant chunks sit near the bottom.

\n
📝 TECHNIQUE\n

Overlap preserves cross-boundary context but inflates index size and duplicates hits; deduplicate by source span before feeding the LLM.

📊 FIGURE — why nobody brute-forces at scale
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Counting the operations

An exact cosine search compares the query against every stored vector, and each comparison is a d-term dot product:

10,000,000 × 768 = 7.68 × 10⁹ multiply-accumulates

Roughly 7.7 billion operations for a single query, before you serve a second user. Even at a few GFLOP/s of effective throughput that is on the order of a second per query — far too slow for interactive search, and it scales linearly with the corpus.

Approximate nearest-neighbour indexes (HNSW, IVF, product quantisation) examine only a small candidate set, cutting the work to roughly logarithmic in N. The cost is recall: they occasionally miss a true nearest neighbour, which is nearly always an acceptable trade.

🎯 EXAM TIP
Exact search over 10M vectors of dimension 768 is about 7.7 × 10⁹ multiply-accumulates per query — N × d, and linear in the corpus size. That single number is the reason ANN indexes exist, and the reason \"just compute cosine similarity against everything\" stops working past a few hundred thousand vectors.

Agent Reliability, Cost, and Complexity

\n

An agent loops: observe → decide → act (tool call) → observe. Because ReAct-style loops resend the full transcript each step, token usage grows quadratically in step count.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
\n
⚙️ FORMULAS\n
    \n
  • End-to-end success with independent steps: P = pᴺ for N steps each succeeding with prob p.
    • \n
  • Growing-context token total ≈ Σᵢ (base + i·Δ) ⇒ O(N²) when history is resent.
    • \n
  • Tree/graph search with branching b and depth d: O(bᵈ) node expansions.
    • \n
  • Expected attempts under retry with success p: 1/p (geometric).
    • \n
\n
💡 KEY RESULTS\n
    \n
  • Reliability compounds multiplicatively: ten 95%-reliable steps yield only ~60% overall success.
    • \n
  • Multi-agent helps when subtasks are parallelizable/independent; it hurts when it adds coordination overhead and error-propagation on tightly-coupled tasks.
    • \n
  • Structured tool-call validation (schema/type checks, retries) is cheaper than letting a malformed call corrupt downstream state.
    • \n
\n
⚠️ SUBTLETY\n

Adding more agents multiplies token cost and introduces new failure surfaces (miscommunication, redundant work); it only pays off when the task truly decomposes.

\n
📝 TECHNIQUE\n

Cap loop iterations and validate every tool output against a schema before acting; treat validation failure as a recoverable step, not a crash.

🧠 The Aistote Method (J-Method)

\n
THE IDEA
The Aistote app is built on two of the most evidence-backed study techniques — active recall and spaced repetition — run in short, intense 25-minute blocks (its \"J-Method\"). Instead of slowly re-reading, you spend the time testing yourself and re-testing what you miss. This app already has every tool the method needs.
\n
THE 3-STEP LOOP
\n\n\n\n
StepWhat you doWhere in this app
1. ConvertTurn the material into questions instead of re-reading it.Open a section, skim the lesson once, then jump to its Quiz.
2. RecallAnswer from memory first — no peeking — then check.Take the section Quiz, or a PA / OA simulation; rate your confidence.
3. Space itRe-test only what you missed, on a growing schedule.Every miss becomes a Flashcard; review them on the app's spaced-repetition schedule.
\n
A 25-MINUTE J-METHOD SESSION
\n\n\n\n\n
TimeDo this
0–3 minSkim the lesson's key terms and the big idea — don't memorize yet, just get the lay of the land.
3–18 minTake the section quiz (or a 15-question drill). Try to recall the answer first, reveal it after.
18–23 minRedo only the questions you got wrong.
23–25 minSend the stubborn ones to Flashcards and note tomorrow's quick review.
\nStart the block with the ⚡ Focus timer (25 min) on any lesson — that is your J-Method session.
\n
⚠️ THE ONE RULE
Always try to answer from memory before you look. The effort of retrieving is what actually builds the memory — re-reading feels productive but barely moves it.
\n
WHY IT WORKS
Active recall (testing yourself) forces your brain to reconstruct the answer, which strengthens it far more than recognition. Spaced repetition reviews each fact just as you're about to forget it, moving it into long-term memory with the fewest reps. The 25-minute block simply makes you actually do both, every day.
\n
DAILY RHYTHM
Two or three 25-minute J-Method blocks a day (new material in one, missed-question review in the next) beats a single long cram session — and it's how the Aistote method delivers \"learn it in 25 minutes\" instead of hours.
